title: Integrated Computational Prioritization and Characterization of Structurally Distinct Putative AT1R Ligands from a Cardiovascular-Focused Chemical Library
content: Hypertension remains a major contributor to the global burden of cardiovascular disease, motivating the exploration of chemically diverse angiotensin II type 1 receptor (AT1R) ligands. This study applied an integrated computer-aided drug design (CADD) workflow to prioritize candidate ligands from a cardiovascular-focused ChemDiv library containing 23,000 compounds. Molecular docking was performed against AT1R (PDB ID: 4ZUD), using olmesartan (PubChem CID: 158781) as the reference ligand. Redocking reproduced the crystallographic pose with an RMSD of 1.01 Å. The 15 highest-ranked compounds based on docking scores were subjected to post-docking MM-GBSA analysis, and nine with more favorable predicted MM-GBSA energy estimates were advanced to physicochemical, pharmacokinetic, drug-likeness, and toxicity assessments. Three compounds (CIDs: 3825369, 53151618, and 71841126) were selected for further characterization using ligand-based structural analysis, density functional theory, exploratory AT2R docking, and 100 ns molecular dynamics simulations. Their docking scores ranged from −9.054 to −9.096 kcal/mol, compared with −8.556 kcal/mol for olmesartan. Fingerprint-based analysis indicated low structural similarity to olmesartan (Tanimoto coefficients: 0.132–0.181). The molecular dynamics analyses revealed compound-dependent differences in conformational behavior and protein–ligand interaction profiles. CID 3825369 and CID 53151618 showed comparatively consistent profiles across the evaluated computational analyses, whereas the results for CID 71841126 showed greater variation in selected dynamic and energetic descriptors. These findings identify structurally distinct computational candidates for further experimental investigation of AT1R ligand activity. However, experimental validation is required to determine receptor binding, functional activity, selectivity, and therapeutic relevance.
